name: Amira Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the hoist crew at a large zinc mine. The hoist lifts ore up the shaft in a big bucket, and I operate the controls when the regular driver is away; most days I check the cable, talk to people below and decide when a lift must wait. I have a two-year technical diploma and have made enough hard stop calls to know a clean schedule can still be wrong. My partner Salim works as a hospital porter, our children are grown, and we have about five months of expenses saved. We hope I can retire at 67. I sometimes use AI to organise service notes after the mechanics have checked the actual parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a tidier service log helps if it leaves the cable inspection with the people who see it. The hoist cannot lift a spreadsheet out of a stuck shaft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead shifts and Salim's hospital wage will carry on. Five months saved is enough for a repair bill, though not enough to throw away a working income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the cable check before the first lift and review a mechanic's signed note before I file it. In the first year I'll try the note-sorting tool on old service sheets, but only after the maintenance team shows me where it makes mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable about our pay. I am willing to try a tool after someone has tested it on a real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the cable inspection catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cable strand frayed near the top wheel last autumn, and we held the hoist while it was replaced. A tidy log would not have shown the loose wire until somebody looked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Salim our usual savings transfer and visits to the grown children can continue. I wouldn't buy a new tablet just to read the same maintenance note.

I would tell the crew a **signed mechanic note** still matters more than polished text.
think: I expect my **lead shifts** and Salim’s hospital wage to continue.
I think our **five-month cushion** handles a repair, but I still need regular work.
do: **Keep checking** the hoist cable before the first lift.
**Try the note sorter** on old service sheets after mechanics show me its errors.
feel: **Comfortable** about pay and open to a tool once it has been tested on shift.

fieldNote: Her **cable inspection** caught a frayed strand that a clean service log could miss.
She uses **AI occasionally**, waiting for mechanics to demonstrate errors before testing a note sorter herself.

steps.text: Keep inspecting the hoist cable before the first lift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and buying may be done by software before the hoist can inspect its own cable. I want operators and mechanics to sign off on new lifting rules together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office side will lose tasks first, and managers might put more lifts into each hour. My lead wage should hold, but a faster schedule can take away the pause needed to check a cable after a jolt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the maintenance lead to show me the new lift-planning screen once it has passed a trial. In the first year I'll compare its proposed pauses with our incident log and take any missing check to the joint safety committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about rushed checks, not about feeding our household next month. A hoist full of ore needs the same careful stop even if the timetable becomes clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you hold a scheduled lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the screen books a lift before we have inspected a jolted cable, I will hold it. The load can wait while a mechanic looks at the strand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What record would help the committee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the newest operator to mark the exact lift number when a check is skipped. I want evidence the committee can use, not a broad complaint.

I would require **operator and mechanic** sign-off on new lifting rules.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to hold while office tasks change.
I worry **faster schedules** could squeeze the cable check after a jolt.
do: **Learn the lift-planning screen** after maintenance has tested it on a real shift.
**Compare planned pauses** with incident logs and bring missing checks to the safety committee.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed cable checks, with household income still secure.
S1.quote: A hoist full of ore needs the same careful stop even if the timetable becomes clever.
fieldNote: She expects **thinking-task changes** in scheduling and buying before capable robots handle hands-on inspection.
Her **AI learning** starts after a real maintenance trial, and the joint committee reviews missed cable checks.

steps.text: Learn the lift-planning screen after a maintenance trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could run schedules and records, while capable hoist robots follow around 2031. We need a negotiated paid path for operators whose shifts could end before their pensions start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, four years before the retirement age Salim and I planned for. Five months saved and one hospital wage would not cover four years of our usual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union for a written count of hoist posts and paid inspection openings this winter. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll take a cable-inspection course only if the mine pays the fee and keeps my wages during training; then I'll apply only for a posted role with comparable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my lead wage, but there is still time to ask for real terms. I do not want my partner working extra hospital shifts to carry a training gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which family plan would you pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Salim we should pause the kitchen renovation until we know the hoist roster. The cupboards can wait; our pension contributions cannot be replaced so easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the instructor to show me the course on a real hoist cable, not only a diagram. If no funded course is offered, I'll keep the current lead shifts as long as they exist.

say: I would distinguish **2028 schedule AI** from capable hoist robots around 2031.
I would seek a **paid operator path** before shifts disappear years ahead of pensions.
think: I think at **63**, I could lose four earning years before planned retirement at 67.
I think five months saved and **one hospital wage** cannot cover our usual bills for four years.
do: **Ask the union** for written hoist post and paid inspection numbers this winter.
**Take cable-inspection training** after thinking AI arrives only with a paid fee and continued wages.
**Pause kitchen renovation** until the mine clarifies the hoist roster.
feel: **Anxious** about lost lead wages, with time to seek negotiated terms.
S2.quote: I do not want my partner working extra hospital shifts to carry a training gamble.
fieldNote: She calculates **2031 robot arrival** at 63, four years ahead of planned retirement at 67.
The **course depends** on a paid fee and maintained wages; any later role also needs a posting and comparable pay.

steps.text: Ask the union for written hoist and inspection post numbers
Take cable-inspection training if mine pays fees and maintains wages
Pause kitchen renovation until the hoist roster is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes planning before capable hoist robots arrive around 2034. A few extra years are useful only if the mine funds practice on the equipment we actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots arrive, one year before we hope to retire. A one-year gap might be covered by our five months of savings and Salim's wage, but I would want pension figures before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the union training officer to identify a cable-inspection certificate accepted by our mine. If the mine funds a place and keeps my wages, I'll enrol next year; in the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a posted inspection role only if pay stays close to my lead wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about one year of income, less cornered than in the fast picture. I can study after a good course is tested, but I will not buy a cable-inspection certificate on a mine promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no inspection vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no inspection vacancy exists, I'll keep leading the hoist crew while the shifts last and compare retirement at 66 with 67. I won't turn the five-month reserve into a whole new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your children the date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children the likely date once the pension statement and the mine's roster are in writing. They shouldn't plan their lives around my guess.

say: I would use the **2034 robot date** to seek real hoist inspection training.
I would require **funded practice** on working equipment before paying attention to a certificate.
think: I think at **66**, I might lose one year of wages before planned retirement.
I think our **five-month cushion** helps, but pension and wage figures must be checked.
do: **Enrol in inspection training** next year only if the mine funds a place and keeps my wages.
**Apply** for a posted inspection role after thinking AI arrives only if pay stays near my lead wage.
**Keep** hoist shifts if no inspection vacancy appears, while comparing retirement at 66 and 67.
feel: **Uneasy** about a possible one-year gap, with a conditional training route.
S3.quote: I will not buy a cable-inspection certificate on a mine promise.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66, one year ahead of hoped-for retirement.
She will **enrol only** with mine funding and wages maintained; any job move requires a posted role and comparable pay.

steps.text: Enrol in cable-inspection training if mine funds a place and maintains wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2036 changes records, while capable hoist robots arrive around 2039. I hope to be retired before either technology changes the lift job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. If our pension at 67 covers the bills, the robot date is a worry for younger operators rather than our own household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading safe hoist shifts and paying into retirement while the roster lasts. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if we are retired as planned, I'll check our pension budget with Salim and speak at the union meeting about paid training for those still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our own income in this picture, provided the pension is enough. I still dislike the idea of a younger operator being offered only an unpaid video course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension comes in low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension comes in low, I would take another posted hoist shift nearby rather than drain savings at once. We have some options, but I would need an offer before changing our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a younger hoist operator learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger operators to learn where the cable bends over the wheel. A screen can show a warning, but a hoist worker still has to know what to inspect.

say: I would expect **2039 hoist robots** after my hoped-for retirement.
I would press for **paid practical training** for younger operators.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if the pension covers our bills.
I could seek **nearby shifts** if a low pension made more mine wages necessary.
do: **Keep leading** safe hoist shifts and paying into retirement while the roster lasts.
Review **pension income** with Salim after 2036; seek a posted nearby hoist shift if income falls short.
**Speak for paid training** at a union meeting after 2036.
feel: **Calm** about household income if pension figures hold, while concerned for younger workers.
S4.quote: A screen can show a warning, but a hoist worker still has to know what to inspect.
fieldNote: Her **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, later than hoped-for retirement at 67.
She pairs **conditional pension security** with union support for paid training, and would require an actual nearby job offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable hoist robots might arrive around 2031, four years before my planned retirement. A funded inspection course with maintained wages and a posted job at comparable pay would help me plan that gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who trains the next hoist operator. An experienced mechanic should stand beside each new hoist operator at the cable wheel. I would teach the screen after that physical check.

headlineQuote: An experienced mechanic should stand beside each new hoist operator at the cable wheel.
portrait: **Amira Jensen**, 58, leads a hoist crew at a large zinc mine after a two-year technical diploma.
She and her partner have **five months saved** and grown children, with his hospital wage supporting their retirement plan.
She uses **AI occasionally** for service notes and learns new tools after mechanics prove them on a shift.
She hopes to **retire at 67**; 2031 robots would leave four earning years at risk, while 2034 robots would leave one.
Her **training and job move** require funded practical instruction, maintained wages and a posted role with comparable pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable hoist robots could arrive four years before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded inspection course** with continued wages and a posted role at comparable pay would help bridge the gap.
